body.text: Vegetarian eating often gets reduced to one question. The fuller pattern deserves more than that.
Start with the whole pattern
Make a week note for staples, vegetables, fruit, grains, beans, lentils, soy foods, dairy foods or alternatives, nuts, seeds, and meals that repeat.
Use categories instead of alarms
The cleanest version is a category list: frequent, occasional, missing, and not sure. It keeps the page calm.
Do not turn one missing category into a health conclusion. A note is not a lab report.
Write fortified foods as context
Fortified foods can be written as part of the pattern when they are already present. This article does not tell you to add a product.
Keep personal needs personal
Pregnancy, breastfeeding, medications, medical conditions, eating history, and individualized plans belong with a licensed professional.

body.text: Delivery meals can be practical. The pattern only gets hard to see when every order feels separate.
Compare the week, not the order
Write a weekly view: repeated meals, vegetables, fruit, protein foods, grains, fluids, and how many meals were eaten in a rush.
Look for repetition
The same lunch four times may be fine. It may also mean a few food groups kept missing. The note can hold that without judgment.
Add what is easy to forget
Fluids, side vegetables, fruit, and sit-down time often disappear quietly. Add them as checkboxes, not corrections.
No app names, no restaurant scores, no lecture. Just a pattern you can actually read.

body.text: Travel can scatter meals without doing anything wrong. Airports, long drives, late arrivals, hotel breakfasts, time zones, family tables: it all counts.
Name the disruption plainly
Write what changed: meal timing, fluids, sleep, caffeine, alcohol, snacks, vegetables, or the simple fact that food was not fully in your control.
Pick one normal anchor
The first anchor can be small: breakfast at home, a familiar lunch, a water bottle on the desk, or dinner before the evening gets away.
No dramatic fresh start. No big speech. Just one ordinary meal that helps the day know where it is.
Let the week settle
Give the record a few days before judging it. Travel leaves loose ends, and not all of them are about food.
If travel affected a medical condition, medication schedule, or personal nutrition plan, follow guidance from a licensed professional.
This article is general education only and is not medical advice.

body.text: Period-week notes need careful language. Food can be part of the record without becoming a period-care plan.
Use cycle timing as context
Write the day of the cycle if you know it, then meals, fluids, sleep, stress, movement, appetite, and cravings.
Write cravings and appetite carefully
Cravings are not a failure. Appetite changes are not a character note. They are lines on the page.
The safest sentence is plain: this changed around the same time as my period. It does not say food caused it or fixed it.
Do not turn food into period care
This article does not tell you what to eat for pain, mood, flow, or cycle changes. Keep individualized questions with a licensed professional.
Escalate worrying changes
If pain, bleeding, cycle changes, weakness, dizziness, or distress are severe, new, persistent, or worrying, seek professional support.

body.text: One week. One page. No detective wall.
Use one page
Make columns for energy, sleep, digestion, thirst, mood, focus, meals, fluids, movement, stress, and anything unusual.
Track signals beside routines
Put body signals beside daily routine, not above it. A short night, skipped lunch, travel day, or hard week belongs on the same page.
Circle patterns, not causes
Circle repeats: three late lunches, two rough nights, vegetables missing, thirst showing up often. Do not write a medical label in the margin.
A weekly page can show what to notice next. It should not decide what is happening inside your body.
Know when the page is not enough
If a signal is severe, sudden, persistent, painful, frightening, or worrying, bring it to a licensed professional.
